parts.problemMd:
A student wants to take a particularly accurate measurement of the volume of liquid in a measuring cylinder.

Which of the following procedures would make her measurement **less** accurate?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****C**** because:**

- Using a large measuring cylinder means that an increase in the volume of the water would give a small change to the height of the liquid in the measuring cylinder.
- Small changes are more difficult to read accurately than larger changes.
- The student *actually* wants to use the *smallest* measuring cylinder possible to take the measurement.

**A **is incorrect as this would eliminate parallax error, making the measurement more accurate.

**B** is incorrect as this makes the reading more accurate and is standard practice .

**D** is incorrect as a vertical cylinder means the surface of the liquid is exactly perpendicular to the graduations on the side. This makes the measurement more accurate.

parts.problemMd:
A student is timing the rate of cooling of a beaker of water. On a repeat run of the investigation, the student forgets to zero the stopwatch.

The readings on the stopwatch at the start time and the end time are shown in Fig. 1.1

![1-1-3e-measuring-time-stopwatch](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/1-motion-forces-and-energy/1-1-physical-quantities-and-measurement-techniques/assets/006-1-1-3e-measuring-time-stopwatch.png)

Calculate how long it took the beaker to cool.
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****D**** because:**

- Cooling time = end time − start time

- Firstly, consider the minutes

  - 23 − 11 = 12 minutes
- Then consider the seconds

  - 27 − 19 = 8 seconds
- Cooling time = 12 minutes and 8 seconds

It is important to work out the minutes and the seconds separately, because if the number of seconds at the end time is greater than the number of seconds at the start time, you will need to adjust the number of minutes.

Remember that there are only 60 seconds in a minute, so time calculations can't be done easily with decimals.

Another method, would be to convert everything into seconds, do the calculation, and convert the answer into minutes.

parts.problemMd:
**Extended tier only**

Identify the physical quantity that is **not** scalar.
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****C ****because:**

- Scalar quantities have magnitude only

- Weight is a force

  - Forces have both magnitude and direction
- Therefore, weight is a vector quantity

Students commonly confuse weight and mass.

Mass is a measure of the amount of matter in an object, it has magnitude but no direction, therefore it is scalar.

Weight is a force, it has magnitude and direction, therefore it is a vector quantity.

parts.problemMd:

Identify the physical quantity that is a scalar.
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****B**** because:**

- Scalar quantities have magnitude (size) only, whereas vector quantities have both magnitude and direction
- Distance has magnitude only
- Therefore it is a scalar quantity

**Displacement** is a vector quantity because it has both magnitude and direction

parts.problemMd:
A person wishes to roast a chicken. The chicken requires 1 hour and 20 minutes in the oven to be properly cooked.

The oven must be switched on 10 minutes before any food is put in, in order to pre-heat, and reach the correct temperature for cooking.

The chicken needs to be ready at 4:30 pm. At what time must the oven be switched on?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****C**** because:**

- The oven needs to be switched on 1 hr and 30 minutes before putting the chicken in
- 1 hr 20 cooking time + 10 minutes to pre-heat = 1 hr 30
- 4:30 − 1 hr 30 = 3:00 pm

**A** & **B** are incorrect as 4:30 − 1 hr 30 is not 2:00 pm or 2:10 pm

parts.problemMd:
A particularly diligent student wants to measure the volume of some liquid for an experiment. She has two measuring cylinders available, a large 250 ml one and a small 50 ml one. The liquid will fit into either of the two measuring cylinders.

As expected, the liquid forms a meniscus where it touches the sides of either measuring cylinder.

Which cylinder should the student use to get the most accurate result, and from where should she measure the liquid level?

| ** ** | **Measuring cylinder** | **Reading taken from** |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | large | Top of meniscus |
| **B** | large | Bottom of meniscus |
| **C** | small | Top of meniscus |
| **D** | small | Bottom of meniscus |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****D**** because:**

- A smaller measuring cylinder will give a greater height difference between two different volumes of liquid. This makes any small differences much easier to measure.
- Liquid level measurements should always be taken from the bottom of the meniscus.

**A **is incorrect as the large measuring cylinder would make it more difficult to measure small differences in the liquid volume, and readings should not be taken from the top of the meniscus.

**B** is incorrect as the large measuring cylinder would make it more difficult to measure small differences in the liquid volume.

**C** is incorrect as liquid level readings should not be taken from the top of the meniscus.

parts.problemMd:
A student uses a stopwatch to time 40 complete swings of a simple pendulum. The total time taken is 1 minute and 52 seconds.

What is the period of the pendulum?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- The period of a pendulum is the time taken for one complete swing
- To calculate the period, the total time must first be converted into seconds
- There are 60 seconds in 1 minute, so the total time (1 minute and 52 seconds) is:

$\text{total time}=60+52=112\text{s}$

- The period is then found by dividing the total time by the number of swings:

$\text{period}=\frac{\text{total time}}{\text{number of swings}}$

$\text{period}=\frac{112}{40}$

$\text{period}=2.8\text{s}$

> **[exam-tip]**
> Remember to convert all time values to the same unit (seconds) before performing calculations. A common mistake is forgetting to convert minutes to seconds, which would give an incorrect answer. Always check that your final answer has sensible units and magnitude for the quantity being calculated.

parts.problemMd:
A student wants to find the volume of a small, irregularly shaped stone.

Which pieces of apparatus should the student use?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- An irregularly shaped solid cannot have its volume calculated using length measurements, so a ruler alone is not sufficient
- The volume of an irregularly shaped solid can be found by the displacement method:

  - The stone is lowered into a measuring cylinder containing a known volume of water
  - The rise in water level equals the volume of the stone
- This requires a **measuring cylinder** (to measure the water level before and after) and **water **(as the displacement liquid)

**A** is incorrect because a balance measures mass, not volume, and a ruler can only measure the volume of a regularly shaped solid (e.g. a cuboid).

**B** is incorrect because a balance is not needed to find volume by displacement. A balance would be needed to find mass (and then density), but the question only asks about volume.

**D** is incorrect because a ruler cannot measure the volume of water displaced by an irregularly shaped object. A measuring cylinder is needed to read the water level accurately.

parts.problemMd:
A student is trying to see how quickly they can run 5.0 km on a standard 400 m running track.

They reason that, if they know how fast they can run one lap, they can assume they will run at the same speed for 5.0 km, and can calculate their predicted time.

They, correctly, reason that they will not be able to maintain their initial pace throughout the whole 5.0 km, so they decide to time lap 5.

The diagram shows the reading on the stopwatch at the beginning and the end of lap 5.

![q2-hard-mcq-1-1--physical-quantities-and-measurement-techniques-cie-igcse-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/1-motion-forces-and-energy/1-1-physical-quantities-and-measurement-techniques/assets/008-q2-hard-mcq-1-1-physical-quantities-and-measurem.png)

Calculate how long it should take the student to run 5.0 km.
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****B**** because:**

- The student wants to run 5.0 km = 5000 m
- Each lap is 400 m, so the student must run $\frac{5000}{400}$ = 12.5 laps
- The time taken for one lap is 11:10:00 − 9:13:00 = 1:57:00, 1 minute 57 seconds.
- If each of the 12.5 laps takes 1:57 to complete, the total time will be 1:57 x 12.5 = 24:22:50

Remember, when adding times, that there are only 60 seconds in a minute! You cannot add times using decimals on a calculator.

Since 57 s is almost 1 minute, the easiest way to do this calculation is to say 12.5 × 2 mins = 25 mins, then minus the 3 seconds from each of those minutes. 12.5 × 3 s = 37.5 s, 25 min − 37.5 s = 24 min 22.5 s

parts.problemMd:
A boat travels $30 \text{km}$ due east and then $40 \text{km}$ due north.

Which row correctly shows the total distance and displacement magnitude?

|   | Total distance | Displacement magnitude |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | 50 km | 70 km |
| **B** | 70 km | 50 km |
| **C** | 70 km | 70 km |
| **D** | 50 km | 50 km |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- The total distance is the sum of the two journey legs

total distance = 30 + 40

total distance  = 70 km

- The displacement is the straight-line distance from start to finish, found using Pythagoras

$s=\sqrt{30^{2}+40^{2}}$

$s=\sqrt{2500}$

$s=50\text{km}$

**A **is incorrect because** ** it swaps distance and displacement — 50 km is the displacement, not the distance.

**C **is incorrect because it uses the scalar sum for both distance and displacement — displacement cannot simply be added.

**D **is incorrect because it uses the resultant (Pythagoras) for both — the total distance is the sum of the path lengths, not the straight-line result.

parts.problemMd:

  - $\mathrm{average} \mathrm{time}=\frac{79.21}{5}$
  - $\text{average time} = 15.8 \mathrm{s} ( 3 \mathrm{s} . \mathrm{f} . )$
- The second stopwatch reading is only given as a “red herring” in this question.

**A **is incorrect as the correct values have not been used to calculate the average speed.

**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****C**** because:**

- The distance travelled is the area beneath the line on a speed−time graph
- In this case, this is a triangle, and the area can be found like this:

$\mathrm{area} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{triangle}=\frac{1}{2}\times\mathrm{base}\times\mathrm{height}=\frac{1}{2}\times400\times20=4000$

The distance travelled can also be found using the average speed of the vehicle. Its initial speed is 0 m/s, and its maximum speed is 20 m/s. This gives an average speed of 10 m/s.

Using the average speed is only possible when the acceleration is uniform (the object is speeding up or slowing down at a constant rate).

**A** is incorrect as 20 m is a value which could be incorrectly read from the *y*-axis.

You need to be aware that you are just looking at the motion between the two points specified, and so you should not use the starting point of the overall motion (0, 0) in the calculation of the gradient. Using this point could result in calculating incorrect answers **C** or **D**.

parts.problemMd:
A spring balance operates by the compression of a spring. It has been calibrated on the Earth in grams.

A beam balance operates by balancing standard masses against the unknown mass to be measured.

The same unknown mass is measured with each balance on the Earth and on the Moon.

The gravitational field strength on the Earth is greater than that on the Moon.

How would the measurements on the Earth compare with those on the Moon?

| ** ** | **spring balance measurements** | **beam balance measurements** |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | larger on the Earth than on the Moon | larger on the Earth than on the Moon |
| **B** | larger on the Earth than on the Moon | same on the Earth as on the Moon |
| **C** | same on the Earth as on the Moon | larger on the Earth than on the Moon |
| **D** | same on the Earth as on the Moon | same on the Earth as on the Moon |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B because:**

- Gravitational field strength is a measure of the force per unit mass acting on an object in a gravitational field

  - An object’s **mass **is always the **same**, regardless of location
  - The force (**weight**) exerted on the object will be **different **depending on the strength of the gravitational field
- The **spring balance** measures the **weight **of the object but is calibrated to give a reading of mass

  - The Earth’s gravitational field strength is stronger than the Moon’s
  - The object experiences a **greater weight **on the Earth than on the Moon
  - Therefore, measurements using the spring balance will be **larger **on the Earth than on the Moon
  - This eliminates options **C** and **D**
- The** beam balance** measures the **mass **of the object

  - The object has the **same mass** on both the Earth and the Moon
  - Therefore, the measurement using the beam balance will be the **same **on the Earth as on the Moon
  - Therefore, the correct answer is **B**

|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | 0 | 3.0 | 3.0 |
| **B** | 0 | 3.0 | 6.0 |
| **C** | 3.0 | 3.0 | 3.0 |
| **D** | 3.0 | 6.0 | 9.0 |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- When there is no load, the spring is not extended

  - Original length is 3.0 cm
  - This is unchanged under no load
  - Eliminate options **C** and **D**
- When the load is 2.0 N newtons, the total length is 6.0 cm

  - Original length is 3.0 cm
  - Extension = 6.0 − 3.0 = 3.0 cm
- When the load is 4.0 N newtons, the total length is 6.0 cm

  - Original length is 3.0 cm
  - Extension = 9.0 − 3.0 = 6.0 cm
  - Eliminate option **A**

Remember that extension is the length under load **minus** the original load. In the first image, there is no load so the spring is not being stretched. This means its extension is zero.

Velocity and acceleration are both vectors: they have direction as well as a magnitude (size). Whenever the velocity of an object changes, it accelerates.

parts.problemMd:
On the Earth, a spring stretches by 5.0 cm when a mass of 3.0 kg is suspended from one end.

Which mass, on the Moon, would stretch the spring by the same extension?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****D**** because:**

- An object's weight is the gravitational force acting on it due to its mass

- The weight of an object on the Moon is 6 times less than its weight on Earth because the gravitational field strength on the Moon is 6 times weaker

You could also answer this question using the Earth’s gravitational field strength (9.8 N/kg) to work out the size of the force acting on the spring, and then work out the Moon’s gravitational field strength and see which object would produce the same size force. However, it is simpler to think through the overall effect of the lower gravitational field strength as explained above.

parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****C**** because:**

- Moment = force x distance from pivot
- Anticlockwise moments arise from the 10 N force from the pan

  - Anticlockwise moment = F × d = 10 × 0.15 = 1.5 N m
- Clockwise moments arise from the box on the right hand side

  - The beam is 65 cm long, so the box is 50 cm = 0.50 m from the pivot
  - Clockwise moment = F x d = F x 0.50

- If the beam is in equilibrium then the sum of the clockwise moments = the sum of the anticlockwise moments

  - F × 0.50 = 1.5 N m
  - F = $\frac{1.5}{0.5}$ = 3 N
- We, therefore, require six 0.5 N weights to balance the yardarm.

parts.problemMd:
The diagram shows a uniform beam which is balanced on a pivot at its centre. A force $F$ is applied at a distance $x$ to the left of the pivot. A second force $2F$ is applied to the right of the pivot to keep the beam in equilibrium.

![A horizontal beam balanced on a pivot with a downward force F at distance x to the left of the pivot.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/1-motion-forces-and-energy/1-5-moments/assets/001-a-horizontal-beam-balanced-on-a-pivot-with-a-dow.png)

What is the distance of the second force from the pivot?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- For a beam to be balanced (in equilibrium), the total clockwise moment must equal the total anticlockwise moment
- The moment of a force is calculated using the equation:

$\text{moment}=\text{force}\times\text{perpendicular distance from pivot}$

- There is an anticlockwise moment due to the force $F$ at a distance $x$ to the left of the pivot

$\mathrm{anticlockwise} \mathrm{moment}=F\timesx$

- Therefore, to balance the beam, there must be a clockwise moment due to the second force $2F$ at a distance $d$ to the right of the pivot

$\mathrm{clockwise} \mathrm{moment}=2F\timesd$

- Set these expressions equal to each other:

$2F\timesd=F\timesx$

- Rearrange the equation to make $d$ the subject and cancel the $F$ terms:

$d=\frac{F\timesx}{2F}$

$d=\frac{x}{2}$

- This is option** A**

parts.problemMd:
**Extended tier only**

An object of mass $1.2\mathrm{kg}$ is moving with a velocity of $2.0m/s$ when it is acted on by a force of $4.0N$. The velocity of the object increases to $5.0m/s$ in the same direction.

For which period of time does the force act on the object?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****A**** because:**

- The momentum of an object is given by:

$\mathrm{momentum}=\mathrm{mass}\times\mathrm{velocity}$  or $p=mv$

- The change in the momentum of the object $( \Delta p )$ can be found using:

$\begin{array}{ccc} \text{change} in \text{momentum} & = & \text{final momentum} - \text{initial momentum} \end{array}$  or  $\begin{array}{ccc}\Delta p & = & p_{final} - p_{initial}\end{array}$

$\begin{array}{ccc} p_{initial} & = & 1.2 kg \times 2.0 \mathrm{m} \div \mathrm{s} = 2.4 kg \mathrm{m} \div \mathrm{s} \end{array}$

$\begin{array}{ccc} p_{final} & = & 1.2 kg \times 5.0 \mathrm{m} \div \mathrm{s} = 6.0 kg \mathrm{m} \div \mathrm{s} \end{array}$

$\begin{array}{ccc}\Delta p & = & p_{final} - p_{initial} = 6.0 - 2.4 = 3.6 kg \mathrm{m} \div \mathrm{s} \end{array}$

- This allows the impulse equation to be used:

$\begin{array}{ccc} \text{impulse} & = & F \Delta t = \Delta ( m v ) = \Delta p \end{array}$

$\begin{array}{ccc}\Delta t & = & \frac{\Delta p}{F}\end{array}$

$\begin{array}{ccc}\Delta t & = & \frac{3.6 kg \mathrm{m} \div \mathrm{s} }{4.0 \mathrm{N} } = 0.90 \mathrm{s} \end{array}$

Since the mass of the object does not change, the answer can be found more quickly by rearranging the impulse equation directly to $\Deltat=\frac{m\Deltav}{F}$ . The change in velocity $\Deltav$ is 3.0 m/s (5.0 m/s – 2.0 m/s). If you are confident in manipulating equations, use this method.

**B**, **C** and **D** are all incorrect answers, where the equations have not been used correctly.

parts.problemMd:
The law of conservation of energy states that energy cannot be created or destroyed, it can only be transferred from one store to another.

Which of the following statements is true?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is**** A ****because:**

- Total energy in = total energy out

  - The total energy transferred into a system will be equal to the total energy transferred away from a system
- Energy transferred away from a system will be the sum of the useful and wasted energy

  - Therefore, the useful energy and wasted energy transferred away from a system must be equal to the total energy transferred into the system
  - This is answer **A**

parts.problemMd: Which of the following energy transfers is most efficient?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****D**** because:**

- The most efficient energy transfer is the one that produces the greatest percentage of useful energy output, which is the same as saying the lowest percentage of wasted energy output
- Answer **D** has a wasted energy output of **25%**

  - Therefore, it has a useful energy output of **75%**
- Answer **D** has the greatest percentage of useful energy output

  - Therefore, it is the most efficient energy transfer

Which action requires the greatest power output from the fork lift truck.
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****B**** because:**

$power=\frac{workdone}{timetaken}$

And

$workdone=force\timesdistance$

Therefore, lifting the box the furthest vertical distance in the smallest time requires the greatest power.

**A** is incorrect as the time taken is longer.

**C** is incorrect as the distance is less.

Which row in the table represents the combination of force and distance that means the smallest amount of work is done on the trolley?

A man climbs a ladder.

Which quantities can be used to calculate the useful power of the man?

parts.problemMd:
A ball is at rest at the top of a hill.

The ball rolls down the hill.

At the bottom of the hill the ball hits a wall and stops.

Which energy changes occur?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B because:**

- At the top of the hill, the ball has only gravitational potential energy
- As it rolls, this is converted to kinetic energy
- Upon hitting the wall, the ball compresses and heats slightly

  - The kinetic energy is transferred to the internal store of the ball

This question can also be answered by a process of elimination. At the end, the ball has come to a stop, so the final change cannot be to kinetic energy. The ball has also rolled to the bottom of the hill, so the final store cannot be gravitational potential energy.

This leaves options **B** and **C**, and it is clear to see that the ball starts with gravitational potential energy as it is at the top of the hill.

parts.problemMd:
A mass hangs vertically from a spring.

The mass is raised to a point P and is then released.

The mass oscillates repeatedly between point P and a lower point Q.

Which energies alternately increase and decrease throughout the oscillations?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A because:**

- Consider the motion of the mass and spring:

  - When the mass is raised to point P, it gains **gravitational potential energy **
  - When the mass is released, that gravitational potential energy is transferred into **kinetic energy**
  - When the spring begins to stretch, the kinetic energy is transferred into **elastic energy** until it reaches the lower point Q
  - As the mass moves back up to point P, the same energy changes occur in reverse
- Therefore, as the mass oscillates repeatedly between P and Q, energy changes between gravitational potential, kinetic and elastic types

**B** is incorrect because elastic energy is stored in the stretched spring

**C** & **D** are incorrect because internal energy is related to the molecules in a substance rather than its motion

parts.problemMd:
**Extended Tier Only**

A car has 620 kJ of kinetic energy. The car brakes and stops in a distance of 91 m.

What is the average braking force acting on the car?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C because:**

- As the car decelerates, the work done by the brakes is equal to the car’s change in kinetic energy
- The car comes to rest, so the final kinetic energy is zero

$\DeltaE_{k}=W=620000J$

- The work done by the brakes to stop the car is equal to

$\DeltaE_{k}=W=Fd$

- Rearrange for the average braking force F and calculate:

$F=\frac{W}{d}=\frac{620000}{91}=6813$ N

- This is closest to 6800 N, which is option **C**

To answer questions like this, you need to read the information provided in the question carefully. Do not make any other assumptions about the movement of the substances.

You should also know which factors affect the energy stores of objects or substances. For example, the amount of energy in an object’s kinetic energy store depends on mass and velocity, and so kinetic energy would increase if the mass increased or if the velocity increased.

parts.problemMd:
A child runs up a set of stairs four times. The time taken for each run is recorded.

Which time is measured when the child’s useful power is greatest?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****A****, because:**

- The power of a system (or child) is given by the relationship:

$\mathrm{power}=\frac{\mathrm{work} \mathrm{done}}{\mathrm{time} \mathrm{taken}}\mathrm{or}P=\frac{W}{t}$

- The work done (*W*) is exactly the same each time the child runs up the stairs, so the maximum power (*P*) is greatest when the time (*t*) is shortest

To answer the question, you need to understand the factors that affect power, but you do not need to calculate it. Power is work done per unit time, or how much work is done per second.

The work done cannot be calculated, as there is not enough information. Power will depend on the height of the stairs and the mass of the child, neither of which was given. However, these remain constant as the stairs are always the same height and the child always has the same mass. Therefore, only the time is important.

parts.problemMd:
A woman of mass 50 kg has 81 J of kinetic energy.

What is her speed?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****C**** because:**

- The kinetic energy equation is:

$E_{k}=\frac{1}{2}mv^{2}$

- Which can be rearranged to give:

$v^{2}=\frac{2E_{k}}{m}$

- Substitution in the values from the question gives:

$v^{2}=\frac{2\times81J}{50kg}=3.24\,v=\sqrt{3.24}=1.8m/s$

parts.problemMd:
**Extended tier only**

A motor lifts a 500 N load through a height of 3.0 m in 10 s. The electrical energy supplied to the motor is 2250 J.

What is the efficiency of the motor?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Calculate the useful energy output (work done against gravity):

$W = F \times d$

$W = 500 \times 3 . 0 = 1500 \text{J}$

- Calculate the efficiency:

`\text{efficiency} = \frac{\text{useful energy output}}{\text{total energy input}} \times 100\%`

`\text{efficiency} = \frac{1500}{2250} \times 100 = 67\%`

**A** is incorrect because 33% could result from halving the useful energy output (e.g. using 750 J instead of 1500 J).

**C** is incorrect because 75% could result from using an incorrect value for the total energy input.

**D** is incorrect because 85% could result from dividing the total energy input by the sum of the input and the load force, rather than calculating work done.

parts.problemMd:
A ball is dropped from a height above the ground.

Which transfer between energy stores takes place as the ball falls towards the ground?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- As the ball falls, it loses height, and therefore the energy in its gravitational potential store decreases
- The ball speeds up, so the energy in its kinetic store increases
- Therefore, the main transfer between energy stores is:

gravitational potential energy → kinetic energy

**A** is incorrect because chemical energy is not involved in a falling ball. Chemical energy is stored in fuels, food and batteries.

**B** is incorrect because elastic energy is only relevant if the ball deforms (e.g. on impact with the ground), not during free fall through air.

**C** is incorrect because this describes the energy transfer for the opposite motion, i.e. a ball being thrown upwards into the air.

parts.problemMd:

A large truck of mass 5000 kg is travelling at 5.0 m/s. A motorbike has a mass of 200 kg. Both the truck and the motorbike have the same kinetic energy.

What is the speed of the motorbike?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****A**** because **

the equation: kinetic energy = ½ x mass x velocity<sup>2</sup> applies here:

$E_{ktruck}=\frac{1}{2}\times5000\times5.0^{2}=62500J$

$E_{kmotorbike}=62500J\mathrm{so}62500=\frac{1}{2}\times200\timesv^{2}$

$v^{2}=\frac{62500}{0.5\times200}\mathrm{so}v^{2}=625$

$v=\sqrt{625}=25m/s$

parts.problemMd:
**Extended tier only**

A penny is held at the top of Blackpool tower. The penny is released and falls a distance *h* to the ground. It reaches a speed *v* as it falls.

As the penny falls, air resistance causes some of the original energy of the penny to be transferred into the air as heat. Which of the expressions below gives the work done against air resistance?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****C**** because:**

- Two equations are at work here:

  - Gravitational potential energy (GPE) = mass x gravitational field strength x height (mgh)
  - Kinetic energy = ½ x mass x velocity<sup>2 </sup>(½ mv<sup>2</sup>)
- The GPE at the top of the tower is converted into both work done **and** kinetic energy on the way down, so mgh = Work + ½ mv<sup>2</sup>
- Rearranging for work done gives: Work done = mgh - ½ mv<sup>2</sup>

**A** is incorrect as ½ mv<sup>2</sup> is the kinetic energy only

**B** is incorrect as the plus sign should be a minus sign.

**D** is incorrect as mgh is the gravitational potential energy only.

parts.problemMd:

The diagram below shows a wind turbine.

![1-7-mcq-h4](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/1-motion-forces-and-energy/1-7-energy-work-and-power/assets/002-1-7-mcq-h4.png)

What is the change in the kinetic energy if the wind speed is reduced by half?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****B**** because:**

- Kinetic energy =  $\frac{1}{2}$= mass × velocity<sup>2</sup>

  - $E_{K}=\frac{1}{2}mv^{2}$
- If the wind speed is reduced by half then:

  - $E_{K} = \frac{1}{2} m ( \frac{v}{2} ) ^{2}$
  - $E_{K}=\frac{1}{2}m\frac{v^{2}}{2^{2}}$
  - $E_{K}=\frac{1}{2}m\frac{v^{2}}{4}$
  - $E_{K} = \frac{1}{4} ( \frac{1}{2} m v ^{2} )$

If the wind speed is reduced by half, then the kinetic energy is reduced by a factor of 4

- Or $\frac{1}{4}$ of the original *E*<sub>K</sub>
- This is answer** B**

This is really a proportionality question, you need to be familiar with how to solve proportionality questions like this to achieve the top grades at IGCSE.

parts.problemMd:
Two students, X and Y, race up the same flight of stairs. Student X has a greater mass than student Y. They both start from rest and develop the same average power during the race.

Which student reaches the top of the stairs first and why?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- As the students climb the stairs, they do work against gravity
- The work done by each student is equal to the energy transferred to the gravitational potential store, which depends on

  - their weight $( W = m g )$
  - the vertical height climbed
- Since both students climb the same vertical height, the student with the smaller weight (student Y) does less work
- Power is defined as the rate of doing work:

$\text{power}=\frac{\text{work done}}{\text{time}}$

- For the same average power, a smaller amount of work done results in a shorter time to reach the top of the stairs

**A** is incorrect as student X does more work and will therefore take more time to reach the top given the same power output.

**C** is incorrect because time depends on both power and the amount of work to be done; since the work values are different, the times cannot be the same.

**D** is incorrect as student Y actually transfers less energy to their gravitational potential store because they have a smaller weight than student X.

parts.problemMd:
A hydroelectric power station generates electricity. Water stored in a reservoir behind a hydroelectric dam flows through a pipe to a generator below the level of the water. The flow of water makes the generator move and this produces electricity.

Which row gives the name of the energy store in the water in the reservoir and the energy store of the moving generator?

|   | reservoir | generator |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | chemical | kinetic |
| **B** | chemical | hydroelectric |
| **C** | gravitational potential | kinetic |
| **D** | gravitational potential | hydroelectric |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- The water in the reservoir is at a higher level than the generator
- The energy store associated with height above the ground is gravitational potential

  - Therefore, the water behind a hydroelectric dam is a store of **gravitational potential energy**
- As the water flows downwards through the pipe to the generator, its speed increases
- The water then moves through a turbine, which turns the generator
- The energy store associated with movement is kinetic

  - Therefore, energy is transferred to the **kinetic energy** store of the generator

**A **&** B** are incorrect as chemical energy is not involved in hydroelectric power stations; this would be more appropriate for a fossil fuel power station, as fossil fuels (e.g. coal, oil) are stores of chemical energy.

**D** is incorrect as hydroelectric is not an energy store, it is an energy resource for generating electricity.

> **[exam-tip]**
> When answering questions about energy stores and transfers in power stations, think about the physical processes involved step by step. In a hydroelectric power station, water starts high up (gravitational potential energy), falls and speeds up (kinetic energy), then drives turbines connected to generators (kinetic energy). Remember that chemical energy is associated with fuels, not with water stored at height.

$P=1.3pg\times20$

$P=26ρg$

- In the second scenario, the depth is 26 m, the density is ρ and the pressure is *P*<sub>*new*</sub>

$P_{new}=pg\times26$

$P_{new}=26pg$

- The pressure in fresh water at 26 m is equal to the pressure in salt water at 20 m

$P_{new}=P$

- This is option **B**

Labelling variables correctly and assigning the right values to each scenario helps avoid errors in these questions. Sometimes a quick sketch can help ensure you have read the question properly.

**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D because:**

parts.problemMd:
A beaker of water, at its boiling point of 100 <sup>o</sup>C, is heated so that the liquid starts to become a gas, also at 100 <sup>o</sup>C.

Which row of the table correctly compares the liquid phase with the gas phase under these conditions?

|   | **Average distance between the particles** | **Average speed of the particles** |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | the same in the liquid and the gas | the same in the liquid and the gas |
| **B** | greater in the liquid | greater in the gas |
| **C** | greater in the gas | greater in the liquid |
| **D** | greater in the gas | the same in the liquid and the gas |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****D**** because:**

- The particles in a liquid are in contact with each other, while those in a gas are considerably further apart.
- The average kinetic energy of each molecule is related to the temperature of the substance. This means that, if a substance has a higher temperature, its molecules will, on average, have a higher kinetic energy.
- As Kinetic energy = $\frac{1}{2}mv^{2}$, the speed of the molecules will also be greater.
- Since both the liquid water and the gaseous water are *both* at a temperature of 100 <sup>o</sup>C, their molecules both have *the same* kinetic energy, and are travelling at *the same* speed.

Each of the other answers has made at least one error. Liquid particles are *always* closer together than gas particles.

Most students incorrectly think that gas particles have a higher kinetic energy than liquid particles. This is ***only*** true* *if the gas is also at a higher temperature than the liquid (which is usually, but not always, the case)

- This increase in particle motion directly corresponds to an increase in their average kinetic energy, which is observed as a rise in temperature

**A** is incorrect as particles become fixed in position during solidification or freezing, which is a change of state usually caused by a drop in temperature.

**B** is incorrect as the mass of individual particles is a fundamental property and does not change with temperature.

**D** is incorrect as particles typically move further apart when a substance expands due to heating, but this is a consequence of increased kinetic energy and intermolecular forces, not what temperature itself measures or what always happens (e.g., if heated at constant volume).

parts.solutionMd:

- Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the molecules
- When the temperature decreases, the average kinetic energy decreases, so the average speed of the molecules decreases
- Slower molecules hit the walls of the balloon less frequently and with less force
- This means the pressure decreases

**A** is incorrect because the average speed of the molecules is directly related to the temperature. If the temperature decreases, the average speed must also decrease.

**B** is incorrect because the pressure does not stay the same. Slower molecules exert less force on the walls of the balloon, so the pressure decreases.

**C** is incorrect because both the average speed and the pressure decrease when the temperature decreases, not increase.

parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- It is caused by collisions between the relatively large smoke particles and the much smaller, fast-moving air molecules

parts.problemMd:
A syringe is half filled with air and sealed. The plunger is then pulled outwards, causing the volume of the gas to increase.

This is done slowly, so that the expansion happens at a constant temperature.

What happens to the pressure of the gas, and to the speed of the air molecules?

|   | **Pressure inside syringe** | **Speed of air molecules** |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | stays the same | stays the same |
| **B** | increases | decreases |
| **C** | decreases | stays the same |
| **D** | decreases | decreases |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****C**** because**

- The average kinetic energy of the molecules in a substance is proportional to the temperature of the substance. Since the temperature inside the syringe is constant, the average KE per molecule also remains constant.
- Since KE = $\frac{1}{2}mv^{2}$, the speed of the air molecules stays the same.
- Pressure against the inside walls of the container is caused by the air molecules colliding with the walls. They move at the same speed, and so the force of each collision remains the same.
- If the volume of the gas increases, then the same number of air molecules have to collide with a larger surface area of the wall.
- As the volume of the container increases, the area over which this force is exerted also increases.
- $Pressure=\frac{force}{area}$
- This means that the pressure inside the syringe decreases.

The other answers have one or both of the statements incorrect, for the reasons outlined above.

parts.problemMd:
An electric heater supplies $12600J$ of energy to $0.50\mathrm{kg}$ of a liquid. The temperature of the liquid rises from $20^{\circ}C$ to $50^{\circ}C$.

What is the specific heat capacity of the liquid?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Use the equation for specific heat capacity:

$E=mc\Deltaθ$

- Rearrange to find *c*:

$c=\frac{E}{m\Deltaθ}$

- The temperature change is:

$\Deltaθ=50-20=30\text{°C}$

- Substitute the values:

$c=\frac{12600}{0.50\times30}$

$c=840\text{J/(kg °C)}$

parts.problemMd: Of the following modes of thermal energy transfer, which one transfers energy at the greatest speed?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****C ****because:**

- Note that the question asks for **speed** and not **rate**.

You have probably seen classroom experiments that show the speed of conduction (balls held onto a copper bar with wax) and convection (purple dye in a rectangular tube). The ‘speed’ of evaporation doesn’t really make sense.

Do not confuse **rate** with **speed**. The **rate** of energy transfer is the amount of energy transferred per second. It is entirely possible for an object to transfer more energy per second by conduction than by radiation, but the means of travel goes at a faster speed for radiation.

**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****A**** because:**

- The refractive index of a material is given by:

$\text{refractive index} = \frac{ \text{sin} ( \text{angle} of \text{incidence} ) }{ \text{sin} ( \text{angle} of \text{refraction} ) } or \mathrm{n} = \frac{ \text{sin i} }{ \text{sin r} }$

- The angle of incidence (the incoming ray) is 90°− 50° = 40°
- The angle of refraction is 40°

parts.problemMd:
The diagram shows a light ray incident on the boundary between a glass block and air at point O.

![A light ray enters the curved edge of a semicircular glass block. The ray hits the midpoint of the edge at O, and 4 possible refraction paths are shown, labelled A, B, C, D.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/3-waves/3-2-light/assets/002-a-light-ray-enters-the-curved-edge-of-a-semicirc.png)

The angle of incidence $i$ is $25 ^{\circ}$. The critical angle for the glass is $42 ^{\circ}$.

Which path does the light ray take after point O?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- When light travels from an optically denser medium (glass) to a less dense medium (air), it refracts away from the normal
- Total internal reflection only occurs if the angle of incidence is greater than the critical angle
- In this case, the angle of incidence ($25 ^{\circ}$) is less than the critical angle ($42 ^{\circ}$), so the light will refract out into the air
- Path **B** shows the ray bending away from the normal as it enters the air

**A** is incorrect as it shows the ray bending towards the normal.

**C** is incorrect as the light only travels along the boundary if the angle of incidence is exactly $42 ^{\circ}$.

**D** is incorrect as total internal reflection only occurs if the angle of incidence is greater than $42 ^{\circ}$.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Remember the key rule: when light passes from a denser to a less dense medium, it bends away from the normal. Always compare the angle of incidence to the critical angle first:
> 
> - if the angle of incidence is less than the critical angle $( i < c )$, refraction occurs
> - if the angle of incidence is equal to the critical angle $( i = c )$, light travels along the boundary
> - if the angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle $( i > c )$, total internal reflection occurs

parts.solutionMd:

  - Therefore, options **C** and **D** can be eliminated
- The closer the object is placed to the lens, the larger the size of the image

  - Therefore, the image produced when the object is at point Q will be inverted and enlarged compared to when the object is at point P

The difficult part of the question is ignoring the rays drawn on the diagram for the object at point P, as the question asks you to move it to point Q. The rays shown give an inverted image that is diminished (smaller), but this is not what the question asks about.

parts.problemMd:
A student uses a thin converging lens with a focal length $f$ of $10 \text{cm}$ to produce a real, inverted, and magnified image of an object.

Where must the object be placed?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- The characteristics of an image formed by a converging lens depend on the position of the object relative to the focal length $f$
- To produce a real, inverted, and magnified image, the object must be placed between $f$ and $2f$
- In this case, $f=10\text{cm}$ and $2f=20\text{cm}$, so the object distance must be between $10\text{cm}$ and $20\text{cm}$
- Therefore, the distance must be $15\text{cm}$ from the lens, which is option **C**

**A** is incorrect because placing the object closer than $f$ ($5 \text{cm}$) would produce a virtual, upright, and magnified image.

**B** is incorrect because when an object is exactly at the focal point $f$ ($10 \text{cm}$), the rays emerge parallel and no image is formed.

**D** is incorrect because when the object is beyond $2 f$ ($25 \text{cm}$), the image formed is real and inverted, but it is diminished (smaller).

> **[exam-tip]**
> Remember the key positions for a converging lens:
> 
> - objects placed closer than $f$ give virtual, upright, magnified images
> - objects between $f$ and $2 f$ give real, inverted, magnified images
> - objects beyond $2 f$ give real, inverted, diminished images
> 
> A quick sketch of ray diagrams for each region can help you visualise and remember these relationships.

An object is placed 9 cm in front of a thin converging lens. The scale diagram shows how the lens forms a real, inverted image.

![A ray diagram showing an object on the left side of a converging lens. Two rays are drawn from the top of the object: one passing through the centre of the lens undeviated, and one parallel to the principal axis refracting through the focal point on the other side. The image is formed where the rays meet, on the right side of the lens, inverted and smaller than the object. An arrow indicates that a large grid square is equal to 6.0 cm.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/3-waves/3-2-light/assets/001-a-ray-diagram-showing-an-object-on-the-left-side.png)

Which row gives the focal length of the lens and the distance of the image from the lens?

|   | focal length of lens / cm | distance of image from lens / cm |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | 6.0 | 18.0 |
| **B** | 9.0 | 12.0 |
| **C** | 12.0 | 9.0 |
| **D** | 18.0 | 6.0 |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- The scale on the diagram shows that 1 large grid square represents a distance of $6 . 0 \text{cm}$
- The focal length is the distance between the centre of the lens and the principal focus
- A ray that travels parallel to the principal axis refracts and passes through the principal focus on the other side of the lens
- On the diagram, the parallel ray crosses the principal axis exactly 1 large square from the centre of the lens, so the focal length is:

$\text{focal length}=1\times6.0=6.0\text{cm}$

- The image is formed where the two rays meet
- The horizontal distance from the centre of the lens to the image is 3 large squares, so the distance of the image from the lens is:

$\text{distance of image}=3\times6.0=18.0\text{cm}$

> **[exam-tip]**
> Remember the two standard rays used to locate an image for a converging lens. A ray travelling through the optical centre of the lens does not change direction. A ray travelling parallel to the principal axis will refract and pass through the principal focus. Identifying these rays will help you locate the principal focus and measure the focal length accurately.

parts.problemMd: Visible light has wavelengths in the range $4.0\times10^{-7}m\mathrm{to}7.0\times10^{-7}m$.What is the range of the frequencies of visible light?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****D**** because:**

- The frequency of a wave can be found using:

$\mathrm{wave} \mathrm{speed}=\mathrm{frequency}\times\mathrm{wavelength} \mathrm{or}v=\mathrm{fλ}$

- This equation can be rearranged to give:

$f=\frac{v}{λ}$

- The speed of light is 3.00 × 10<sup>8</sup> m/s so the frequencies can be found like this:

$f_{max}=\frac{3.00\times10^{8}m/s}{4.0\times10^{-7}m}=7.5\times10^{14}\mathrm{Hz}\,\,f_{\mathrm{min}}=\frac{3.00\times10^{8}m/s}{7.0\times10^{-7}m}=4.3\times10^{14}\mathrm{Hz}$

- This gives a range of  to $4.3\times10^{14}\mathrm{Hz} \mathrm{to}7.5\times10^{14}\mathrm{Hz}$

**A** and **B** incorrect as the powers (×10<sup>8</sup> etc.) have not been used correctly to reach this answer.

parts.problemMd:

parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****C**** because:**

  - But in the solutions above the units are either **cm/s** or **km/s**
- There are 1 000, or 10<sup>3</sup> metres in one kilometre, therefore the speed in km / s = (3.0 × 10<sup>8</sup> m/s) ÷ 10<sup>3</sup> = 3.0 × 10<sup>5</sup> km/s

  - Option **D** is not correct
- There are 100, or 10<sup>2</sup> centimetres in one metre therefore the speed in cm / s = (3.0 × 10<sup>8</sup> m / s) × 10<sup>2</sup> = 3.0 × 10<sup>10</sup> cm/s

  - Option **C** is correct

Converting large and small numbers and units is a key skill for the Physics or Engineering student. This question is getting you to practice working with indices so that you can easily convert between cm, m and km.

parts.problemMd:
A student stands at a distance $d$ from a wall. He claps his hands and hears an echo $1.2\text{s}$ later.

What is the approximate value of $d$?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- The sound travels from the student to the wall and then back again to be heard as an echo
- The speed of sound in air is about $330m/s$
- The total distance travelled by the sound is calculated using the equation:

$\text{total distance}=\text{speed}\times\text{time}$

$\text{total distance}=330\times1.2=396\text{m}$

- The distance $d$ to the wall is exactly half of the total distance travelled by the sound:

$d=\frac{396}{2}=198m$

- This is approximately equal to $200m$, which is option **C**

**A** is incorrect as this corresponds to a speed of sound of $\frac{50\times2}{1.2}\approx83m/s$, which is too low.

**B** is incorrect as this corresponds to a speed of sound of $\frac{100\times2}{1.2}\approx167m/s$, which is too low.

**D** is incorrect as this corresponds to a speed of sound of $\frac{400\times2}{1.2}\approx667m/s$, which is too high.

> **[exam-tip]**
> When dealing with echo questions, always remember that the sound travels twice the distance to the reflecting surface — once going and once returning. A common mistake is to forget to halve the total distance calculated. Make sure you identify whether the question asks for the one-way distance or the total distance travelled by the sound.

![q5-hard-mcq-4-1-simple-phenomenaof-magnets-cie-igcse-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/4-electricity-and-magnetism/4-1-simple-phenomena-of-magnetism/assets/015-q5-hard-mcq-4-1-simple-phenomenaof-magnets-cie-i.png)

The rod is attached to the south pole of a permanent magnet, and then paper clips are attached to the rod. The number of paper clips that can be held by the rod is counted.

The permanent magnet is then removed from the rod, and the number of paper clips that remain attached are counted.

The results are summarised in the table below.

Which of the rods becomes the strongest permanent magnet?

| **rod** | **number of paper clips held by the rod** |   |
|---|---|---|
| **when the magnet is present** | **when the magnet is removed** |   |
| **A** | 5 | 2 |
| **B** | 4 | 3 |
| **C** | 2 | 0 |
| **D** | 3 | 2 |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****B**** because**

- The strongest permanent magnet is able to hold the most paper clips when the bar magnet is taken away, regardless of how many it held when the bar magnet was present.
- Rod **B** can hold the most paper clips.

Each of the other rods holds fewer paperclips when the permanent magnet is taken away.

parts.problemMd: What is the unit of electromotive force?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****B**** because: **

- The unit of electromotive force (EMF) is the volt.

**A **is incorrect as the joule is the unit of energy.

**C **is incorrect as the ampere is the unit of current.

**D **is incorrect as the watt is the unit of power (there’s a great physics joke here, “Watt (what) is the unit of power?” to which the correct answer is “yes, it is”...!

Which line identifies the possible charges on **X** and **Y**?

|   | **X** | **Y** |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | neutral | neutral |
| **B** | negative | negative |
| **C** | negative | positive |
| **D** | positive | negative |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****B**** because:**

- When objects are charged, **like** charges **repel** and **opposite** charges **attract**

  - Neutrally charged objects do not exert a force on each other
- The two balls are suspended far apart

  - Therefore there must be a force between them, which is repelling them (pushing them apart)
- The only option with two like charges is **B**

parts.problemMd: Which line correctly states the equation for **electrical energy**?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****D**** because:**

- Electrical energy = power × time
- Power = current × voltage
- Therefore, the correct energy equation is:

Which unit is equivalent to a volt (V)?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B because:**

- A volt (V) is equivalent to the energy transferred per unit of charge, which is a joule per coulomb, or J/C

**A **is incorrect because a volt is equivalent to current multiplied by resistance (AΩ), not current divided by resistance (A/Ω)

**C **is incorrect because joules per second (J/s) is equivalent to the watt (W), which is the unit of power

**D **is incorrect because a volt is equivalent to the energy transferred per unit of charge (J/C), not the power per unit of charge (W/C)

parts.problemMd: Which particles move to cause a current in a copper wire?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****B****, because:**

- Metals like copper contain free electrons, which can move
- Electrons have an electric charge. When charges move, an electric current is formed

Metallic bonding releases some of the electrons from the metal atoms, these are free to move through the metal.

**A** is incorrect as copper atoms are neutral and their movement could not cause an electric current. Copper atoms also cannot flow with a solid metal.

**D** is incorrect as neutrons are neutral, and their movement could not cause an electric current.

**C** is incorrect as protons cannot leave copper nuclei to form a current.

parts.problemMd:
A wire has a uniform circular cross-sectional area.

Which statement is correct?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****C**** because:**

- Longer wires have greater resistance
- The resistance of a wire is directly proportional to its length. For example, tripling the length of the wire will triple its resistance

  - Therefore, eliminate option **B**
- Thicker wires (ones with larger diameters) have lower resistance
- The resistance of a wire is inversely proportional to its cross-sectional area. For example, halving the cross-sectional area will double the resistance

  - Therefore, eliminate options **A** and **D**

Be careful not to confuse cross-sectional area and diameter here. Resistance decreases as diameter increases, but these quantities are not inversely proportional.

parts.problemMd:
The diagrams show the voltage–time graphs for two electrical power supplies, X and Y.

![Graph X shows a horizontal line at a constant positive voltage. Graph Y shows a sine wave where the voltage oscillates between positive and negative values / time.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/4-electricity-and-magnetism/4-2-electrical-quantities/assets/001-graph-x-shows-a-horizontal-straight-line-at-a-co.png)

Which row correctly identifies the type of current provided by each supply?

|   | **supply X** | **supply Y** |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | alternating current (a.c.) | direct current (d.c.) |
| **B** | alternating current (a.c.) | alternating current (a.c.) |
| **C** | direct current (d.c.) | direct current (d.c.) |
| **D** | direct current (d.c.) | alternating current (a.c.) |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- Direct current (d.c.) is a flow of charge that travels in one direction only, meaning the voltage remains on one side of the zero line (usually constant)
- Alternating current (a.c.) is a flow of charge that continuously reverses its direction, which is shown on a graph by the voltage moving between positive and negative values
- Supply X shows a constant positive value, identifying it as d.c.
- Supply Y shows a wave that crosses the zero line, identifying it as a.c.

**A** is incorrect as it reverses the identification of both graphs.

**B** is incorrect as graph X does not reverse its direction.

**C** is incorrect as graph Y clearly shows the voltage changing polarity (alternating).

> **[exam-tip]**
> When interpreting voltage–time graphs, remember that d.c. stays on one side of the zero line (constant polarity), while a.c. crosses the zero line repeatedly (changing polarity). A quick way to identify a.c. is to look for a waveform that oscillates above and below zero.

parts.problemMd: The electromotive force (e.m.f.) of a battery is
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- The electromotive force (e.m.f.) of a source is defined as the energy transferred per unit charge in driving charge around a complete circuit
- It is measured in volts (V), where 1 V = 1 J/C
- The e.m.f. represents the total energy the battery gives to each coulomb of charge

**A** is incorrect because this is the definition of current ($I=Q/t$), not e.m.f.

**C** is incorrect because, despite the word "force" in its name, e.m.f. is not a force. It is an energy transfer per unit charge. This is a common misconception.

**D** is incorrect because this describes the terminal potential difference when no current flows, which happens to equal the e.m.f. numerically. However, this is not the definition of e.m.f. — it is a consequence of there being no internal energy losses.

parts.problemMd:
A PVC (plastic) rod is rubbed with a nylon cloth. This process causes electrons to be transferred between the rod and the cloth, causing both objects to become charged.

Which row gives the correct nature of the charges on both the cloth and the rod, and the effect the objects have on each other after becoming charged?

|   | **Charges on rod and cloth** | **Effect** |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | the same | repel |
| **B** | the same | attract |
| **C** | opposite | repel |
| **D** | opposite | attract |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****D**** because:**

- When the rod is rubbed with the cloth, electrons are transferred between them

  - If electrons move from the cloth, the cloth becomes positive
  - If electrons move to the rod, the rod becomes negative

- This means the two objects have **opposite **charges
- Opposite charges **attract**

**A **and **B** are incorrect as the charges will be opposite.

**C **is incorrect as opposite charges will attract, not repel.

parts.problemMd:
A student wants to charge up some rods by rubbing them with a cloth made from a suitable material.

He has a number of rods to choose from: a copper rod, a PVC rod, an aluminium rod and a glass rod.

Which two of the rods would hold a charge when rubbed with an appropriate cloth?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****D**** because:**

- Electrical conductors cannot hold a charge when rubbed by a cloth, as electrons very quickly flow into (or out of) them from whatever is touching them.
- Therefore, only **electrical** **insulators** can be **charged** by **rubbing**. Glass and PVC are electrical insulators. Aluminium and copper are not.

**A **is incorrect as aluminium is an electrical conductor.

**B **is incorrect as copper is an electrical conductor.

**C **is incorrect as both aluminium and copper are electrical conductors.

parts.problemMd:

A student considers how changing the diameter and length of a wire affects its resistance.

Which row shows the changes that could be made to the length and diameter of the wire to **decrease** its resistance?

|   | **Change to length** | **Change to diameter** |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | increase | increase |
| **B** | increase | decrease |
| **C** | decrease | increase |
| **D** | decrease | decrease |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****C**** because:**

- The resistance of a wire is **directly** **proportional** to its **length**

  - Therefore, a **shorter **wire would give a lower resistance

- The resistance of a wire is **inversely** **proportional** to its **diameter**

  - Therefore, a **larger **diameter wire would give a lower resistance

**A **is incorrect as increasing the length would increase the resistance of the wire.

**B **is incorrect as both of these factors would increase the resistance of the wire.

**D **is incorrect as decreasing the diameter would increase the resistance of the wire.

parts.problemMd:
A student rubs an acetate rod with a cloth, giving it a negative charge. She then holds it near an earthed, conducting sphere as shown in the diagrams below.

Which diagram shows the correct distribution of charges on the conducting sphere?

![q3-medium-mcq-4-2-electrical-quantitiescie-igcse-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/4-electricity-and-magnetism/4-2-electrical-quantities/assets/011-q3-medium-mcq-4-2-electrical-quantitiescie-igcse.png)
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****D**** because:**

- The rod is negatively charged, and the sphere is earthed (grounded)
- The negative charges in the rod **repel **the negatively charged electrons in the sphere
- The electrons move away from the surface, **along **the earth wire and **away **from the conducting sphere
- This leaves the conducting sphere with a net **positive **charge concentrated on the side nearest the negative rod

**A & C** are incorrect as they show negative charges on the sphere. This would only happen if the sphere were not earthed. Since there is an earth connection, the excess negative charge leaves the sphere.

**B** is incorrect as it shows a uniform distribution of positive charge and misses the fact that the negative rod would cause the positive charge to be concentrated on the side nearest the rod only.

Remember, the positive protons never move, only electrons do. When the negative electrons are repelled by the negatively charged rod, they move away from the protons, leaving an overall positive charge.

Which of the following wires has the largest resistance?

|   | **Length of wire / cm** | **Diameter of wire / mm** |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | 100 | 0.2 |
| **B** | 300 | 0.1 |
| **C** | 50 | 0.4 |
| **D** | 30 | 0.5 |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****B**** because:**

- The resistance of a wire is **proportional **to its **length**

  - Therefore, the **longest** wire will have the highest resistance

- The resistance of a wire is **inversely** **proportional** to its **diameter**

  - Therefore, the **narrowest** wire will have the highest resistance

- Wire **B** has both the longest length and the smallest diameter, hence it has the greatest resistance

None of the other wires have that winning combination of being the longest wire or having the smallest diameter.

parts.problemMd:
A water heater is connected to a 230 V supply and there is a current of 26 A in the heater.

It takes 20 minutes to heat the water to the required temperature.

How much energy is supplied by the heater?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D because:**

- Electrical power is the product of current and potential difference

$P=IV$

- Energy supplied over a period of time is the product of power and time

$E=Pt$

$E=IVt$

- Convert 20 minutes to seconds

$t=20mins=20\times60=1200s$

- Substitute the known quantities into the equation for energy

$E=26\times230\times1200=7176000J$

- Convert this value to standard form

$E=7.18\times10^{6}J$

- This rounds to option **D**

parts.problemMd:
Four students draw a circuit diagram of the apparatus used to measure the resistance of resistor R.

Which circuit is correct?

![Circuits](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/4-electricity-and-magnetism/4-2-electrical-quantities/assets/003-circuits.png)
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****D****, because:**

- Resistance can be calculated using current and voltage measurements of a component
- The ammeter must be placed in series with the component being tested

  - Therefore, circuits **A** and **C** can be eliminated
- The voltmeter must be placed in parallel with the component being tested, and only with that component

  - Therefore, circuit B can be eliminated
- This leaves the correct circuit **D**

The ammeter must be placed in series to measure the current *through* the component being tested and the voltmeter must be in parallel to measure the voltage *across* the component. Look at the circuits carefully to make sure that the voltmeter is only measuring the voltage across the component being tested, not other components as well.

**A** is incorrect, as the ammeter is placed in parallel with resistor R and the voltmeter is placed in series with resistor R.

**B** is incorrect, as the voltmeter is in parallel with resistor R and the variable resistor. The ammeter is correctly placed.

**C** is incorrect, as the ammeter is in parallel with resistor R (and the variable resistor) and the voltmeter is in series with resistor R.

** **A battery is connected to a circuit. It is switched on for 1.0 minute. During that time, there is a current of 0.40 A in the circuit and the battery supplies a total of 48 J of energy.

Which row gives the charge that passes and the electromotive force (e.m.f.) of the battery?

|   | charge that passes in 1.0 minute / C | e.m.f. of the battery / V |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | 0.40 | 2.0 |
| **B** | 0.40 | 120 |
| **C** | 24 | 2.0 |
| **D** | 24 | 120 |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****C**** because:**

- The amount of charge transferred is given by:

$\mathrm{current}=\frac{\mathrm{charge} \mathrm{transferred}}{\mathrm{time}}=\mathrm{or}I=\frac{Q}{T}\,Q=It=0.40A\times60s=24C$

- The e.m.f. of the battery is given by:

$e.m.f.=\frac{\mathrm{energy} \mathrm{transferred}}{\mathrm{charged} \mathrm{transferred}}=\mathrm{or}E=\frac{W}{Q}\,E=\frac{W}{Q}=\frac{48J}{24C}=2.0V$

parts.problemMd:
An electric heater with a power rating of $2000\text{W}$ is switched on for $3.0\text{hours}$. The cost of $1\text{kWh}$ of electricity is $20\text{cents}$.

What is the total cost of using the heater?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- To calculate the cost, the electrical energy used must first be found in kilowatt-hours $( kWh )$
- The power $P$ of the heater must be converted from watts $( \mathrm{W} )$ to kilowatts $( kW )$ by dividing by $1000$

$P=\frac{2000}{1000}=2.0\text{kW}$

- The electrical energy $E$ used is calculated by multiplying power $P$ in $\text{kW}$ by the time $t$ the heater is switched on, which is $3.0h$

$E=Pt$

$E=2.0\times3.0=6.0\text{kWh}$

- The total cost of using the heater is the electrical energy $E$ used multiplied by the cost per unit, which is $20\mathrm{cents}/\mathrm{kWh}$

$\text{total cost}=6.0\times20=120\text{cents}$

> **[exam-tip]**
> Remember to always convert power from watts to kilowatts before calculating energy in kWh. A common mistake is forgetting this conversion, which leads to an answer that is 1000 times too large.
> 
> The formula to remember is:
> 
> Cost = Power (kW) × Time (h) × Cost per kWh
> 
> Make sure you keep track of your units throughout the calculation to avoid errors.

$text power end text ( P ) = text current end text ( I ) \times text voltage end text ( V )$

- Rearranging for current $I$:

$I=\frac{P}{V}$

$I=\frac{2100}{240}=8.75\text{A}$

- A fuse must have a rating that is higher than the normal operating current so it does not blow during regular use
- To provide the best safety protection, the fuse rating should be the smallest available value that is still higher than the calculated current
- The $10 \text{A}$ fuse is the smallest available rating that is greater than $8 . 75 \text{A}$

**A** is incorrect as a $3 \text{A}$ fuse is much lower than the operating current and would blow immediately.

**B** is incorrect as a $5 \text{A}$ fuse is lower than the $8 . 75 \text{A}$ required by the hairdryer.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Always select the fuse with the smallest rating that is still greater than the calculated current. Many students incorrectly choose a fuse that is too high (e.g. $13 \text{A}$) because it would still work, but remember that the purpose of a fuse is to protect the circuit — a fuse rated too high offers less protection against faults.

**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****A**** because:**

- There are two ways to approach this question: calculating the current, and then using *V* = *IR* separately on each resistor, or by using ratios.
- By Ratios:

  - Note that the resistance is split in a 1:3 ratio. The voltage will also split in this way.
  - To calculate this we first total the resistance, 10 + 30 = 40 Ω, and then divide each of our resistances by the total:
  
    - 10/40 = 0.25
    - 30/40 = 0.75
  - Finally, we multiply the 8.0 V supply voltage by our fraction to calculate the voltage across each resistor.
  - V across the 10 Ω resistor = 8.0 x 0.25 = 2.0 V

- By calculating the current:

  - Determine the total resistance of the circuit: 30 + 10 = 40 Ω
  - Determine the current, $I=\frac{V}{R}=\frac{8.0}{40}=0.20A$
  - Use Ohm’s law for the resistor across which you want to find the potential difference: *V* = *IR* = 0.20 x 10 = 2.0 V

| **C** | stays the same | increases |
| **D** | stays the same | stays the same |

parts.problemMd:
The diagram shows a potential divider circuit. A power supply is connected in series with a $6.0Ω$ resistor and an $8.0Ω$ resistor.

A voltmeter connected across the $8.0Ω$ resistor reads $12V$.

![A circuit diagram showing a power supply connected to two resistors in series. The first resistor is labelled 6.0 Ω and the second is labelled 8.0 Ω. A voltmeter is connected across the 8.0 Ω resistor.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/4-electricity-and-magnetism/4-3-electric-circuits-and-electrical-safety/assets/001-a-circuit-diagram-showing-a-power-supply-connect.png)

What is the electromotive force (e.m.f.) of the power supply?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- First, use Ohm's law to determine the current flowing through the $8.0Ω$ resistor
- Rearrange for $I$ and substitute the potential difference ($12 \text{V}$) and resistance ($8.0Ω$) into the equation:

$V=IR$

$I=\frac{V}{R}=\frac{12}{8.0}$

$I=1.5\text{A}$

- In a series circuit, the current is the same at all points, so $1 . 5 \text{A}$ also flows through the $6.0Ω$ resistor and the power supply
- The potential difference across the $6.0Ω$ resistor is:

$V=I\timesR$

$V=1.5\times6.0=9.0\text{V}$

- The e.m.f. of the power supply is equal to the sum of the potential differences across all components in a series circuit:

$\text{emf}=12+9.0=21V$

**A** is incorrect as this is only the potential difference across the $6 . 0  Ω$ resistor, not the total e.m.f. of the power supply

**B** is incorrect because this is simply the sum of the two resistance values, rather than a calculated voltage

**D** is incorrect as it incorrectly calculates the circuit current by dividing the $12 \text{V}$ by the $6 . 0  Ω$ resistor instead of the $8 . 0  Ω$ resistor, which leads to an incorrect total e.m.f. of $28 \text{V}$

> **[exam-tip]**
> Alternatively, you can solve this in one step using the potential divider formula: $V_{\text{out}} = \text{e.m.f.} \times \frac{R_{2}}{R_{1}+R_{2}}$. Substituting the values gives $12 = \text{e.m.f.} \times \frac{8.0}{14.0}$, which rearranges to an e.m.f. of $21 \text{V}$.

![Electrical circuit diagram showing five bulbs labelled P, Q, R, S, T, and U, connected to a battery in parallel and series arrangements.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/4-electricity-and-magnetism/4-3-electric-circuits-and-electrical-safety/assets/008-electrical-circuit-diagram-showing-five-bulbs-la.png)

parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A because:**

- The brightness of a lamp is determined by the power it receives

  - This is dependent on the potential difference and current across each lamp (*P* = *VI*)
- In a series circuit:

  - the potential difference across the components is shared
  - the current through all the components is the same
- Since P, Q&R and S&T&U are in series, the current at a point before P is the same as a point after S&T&U
- In a parallel circuit:

  - the potential difference across each branch is the same
  - the current splits along each branch at a junction
- Lamps R & Q, and lamps S, T & U, are in parallel
- Therefore, the current in P = current in (Q + R) = current in (S + T + U)
- Since the bulbs are identical, lamp P is the brightest as it receives

  - the greatest current
  - the greatest potential difference
  - the maximum power

The combined resistance of two lamps in parallel is less than one individual lamp. This means lamp P has the greatest resistance and, therefore, the greatest share of potential difference.

$\frac{V_{p}}{V_{s}}=\frac{240}{15}=16$

$\frac{N_{p}}{N_{s}}=\frac{1200}{75}=16$

| **B** | N pole | S pole |
| **C** | S pole | N pole |
| **D** | S pole | S pole |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C because:**

- When a magnet is dropped vertically through a solenoid, the induced magnetic pole can be deduced using Lenz’s law
- Lenz’s law states that the direction of an induced e.m.f. always opposes the change causing it
- In diagram 1:

  - The magnet approaches the coil with its south pole closest to the top of the coil
  - Therefore, a **south **pole will be induced at position X to oppose the magnet’s motion by **repelling **it
- In diagram 3:

  - The magnet leaves the coil with its north pole closest to the bottom of the coil
  - A south pole will be induced at the bottom of the coil to oppose the magnet’s motion by **attracting **it
  - Therefore, a **north **pole will be induced at position X (as the coil acts like a bar magnet, so it must have a north and a south pole)
- This is option **C**

$4000\times25000=400000\timesI_{s}$

$I_{s}=\frac{4000\times25000}{400000}=250A$

**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****A ****because: **

- Using Fleming’s left-hand rule:

  - the magnetic field (first finger) points from North to South
  - the current (second finger) points “into the page” in the direction of current flow.
  - the force on the wire (thumb) is directed downwards, in the direction OP

Fleming’s left-hand rule predicts the direction of the force on a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field.

![SpuZdlFb_flemings-left-hand-rule-from-site](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/4-electricity-and-magnetism/4-4-electromagnetic-effects/assets/025-spuzdlfb-flemings-left-hand-rule-from-site.png)

This is a motor effect question, you know because current is already flowing in the wire, and you are asked to predict the direction of the force. If the wire had been pushed, it would be a generator question.

**Top Tip:** if a wire experiences a force without being touched, it’s the motor effect. If the wire is physically dragged through the field, it’s the generator effect.

Actually, the two are equivalent, but that requires slightly deeper thought than we need at IGCSE.

  - Rotate your hand so that your first finger points in the direction of the magnetic field (north to south) and so that your second finger points in the direction of the current in the wire

Thumb indicates motion, first finger shows magnetic field, second finger represents current.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/4-electricity-and-magnetism/4-4-electromagnetic-effects/assets/011-diagram-of-a-left-hand-showing-fleming-s-left-ha.png) Don’t be afraid of using the left-hand rule during an examination. Just put your thumb and first two fingers in the correct positions and align them with the field and current directions in the diagram. Make sure you use your left hand! **A** and **B** are incorrect because these directions are not perpendicular (at right angles) to the direction of the magnetic field. **D** is incorrect because this direction is not perpendicular to the direction of the current.

Arrows indicate axes directions.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/4-electricity-and-magnetism/4-4-electromagnetic-effects/assets/008-graph-showing-a-sinusoidal-wave-with-voltage-bet.png)

![Four diagrams, labelled A to D, show different mechanical lever and piston configurations with labels X and Y on dual pistons below a lever.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/4-electricity-and-magnetism/4-4-electromagnetic-effects/assets/009-four-diagrams-labelled-a-to-d-show-different-mec.png)
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****C**** because:**

- At point P in the graph, the magnitude (size) of the p.d. is greatest
- The coil must be parallel to the magnetic field to produce the maximum p.d. (figures A and C)

  - Therefore, options **B** and **D** can be eliminated
- A positive value of p.d. indicates that X is more positive than Y
- Therefore, a negative value of p.d. indicates that Y is more positive than X

**A** is incorrect as this corresponds to a maximum p.d., but the polarity is opposite (X would be more positive than Y), so it matches a positive peak, not point P, which is a negative peak.
